title: Latrines and cat holes
summary: On the move, dig a cat hole 6 to 8 inches deep at least 200 feet from water, trails and camp; for a group that stays put, dig a pit or trench latrine at least as far from water, downhill and downwind of camp, cover the waste with soil, and close it before it fills.

list: Moving, or a night or two in one place: cat holes (Leave No Trace).
Staying in one camp longer than a few nights, or with young children: a latrine (Leave No Trace).
In town: don’t dig latrines. King County public health says they are not right for urban places, and Jefferson County warns that germs spread easily to neighboring properties. Use the bucket toilet.

blocks.label: Toilets when the water is off

steps: Walk at least 200 feet (60 m) from water, trails and camp: about 70 steps (US Forest Service; Leave No Trace says 70 to 80 adult paces).
Pick a spot where people are unlikely to walk or camp (Leave No Trace).
With a small trowel, dig a hole 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) deep and 4 to 6 inches (10 to 15 cm) across (Leave No Trace, US Forest Service, National Park Service).
When finished, fill the hole with the soil you dug out and cover it with leaves and debris (National Park Service).
With a group, or in one place for more than a night, spread the cat holes over a wide area. Don’t go to the same place twice (Leave No Trace, National Park Service).

blocks.cap: Cat hole: at least 200 feet (60 m) from water, trails and camp (about 70 steps); 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) deep and 4 to 6 inches (10 to 15 cm) across. Fill it with the soil you dug out.

blocks.p: On New York State land in normal times, the rule is a hole 6 to 8 inches deep at least 150 feet from water or campsites, covered with leaves and soil; use a pit privy where one is provided (NYS DEC). DEC notes that Leave No Trace recommends 200 feet.

list: Pack used toilet paper out in a sealed bag: a zipper bag inside another zipper bag (National Park Service, US Forest Service). Leave No Trace also allows burying it deep in the cat hole.
Always pack out wipes, even ones sold as biodegradable (Leave No Trace).
Don’t burn toilet paper: it can start a wildfire (Leave No Trace).
Unscented paper is better (Leave No Trace).

blocks.p: Pee at least 200 feet (60 m) from trails, campsites and water (Leave No Trace). Pee on rocks, pine needles or gravel: animals come for the salt and dig up plants and soil. Pouring some water over it helps (Leave No Trace).

Some places require you to carry all solid waste out; land managers can tell you the rules for an area in normal times (Leave No Trace). Seal it tight in zipper bags or a plastic container (National Park Service), or use a commercial pack-out bag (Leave No Trace).
A latrine holds a lot of waste in one spot and it breaks down slowly, so where you put it matters most (Leave No Trace).

head: Keep the latrine
Distance
rows: From streams, lakes, ponds, springs and wells
At least 200 feet (60 m). This app uses the cat-hole distance (Leave No Trace, US Forest Service). King County, Oregon State Extension and the Sphere handbook give 100 feet (30 m).
From tents, homes and the kitchen
Bottom of the pit at least 5 feet (1.5 m) above it (Sphere handbook). King County gives 1 foot (30 cm).

list: Put it downhill from wells and springs (King County), never uphill or upwind of camp (Sphere handbook).
Where the groundwater is near the surface, a pit latrine is not suitable (CDC). If water seeps into the hole as you dig, it is too near: fill the hole and pick higher ground.
In limestone or broken (fissured) rock, go farther from water than the table says (Sphere handbook).
Keep it away from where food is prepared and eaten (King County).

steps: Dig the hole at least 3 feet (90 cm) deep (King County).
After each use, throw in soil, mulch or ash (King County). A handful of soil after each use speeds breakdown and cuts smell (Leave No Trace).
Cover the latrine between uses with plywood or something similar, and keep covers and doors closed to keep out insects and animals (King County).
Put a place to wash hands with soap and water right next to it (King County, Sphere handbook, CDC).
Watch small children when they use it (King County).

blocks.p: A trench latrine is quick to dig: a narrow trench with a screen for privacy. Cover the waste with soil at least once every day, and dig a small ditch to steer rain water around it. It doesn’t last long, and rain can flood it (CDC). Use the same distances as the table above.

steps: Close it when the waste is about 20 inches (0.5 m) from the top (Sphere handbook leaves 0.5 m for backfill; the US Army closes at 1 foot).
Fill it to ground level with soil, packing it down as you go (US Army field sanitation; CDC: cover with soil when near full).
Mound more soil on top to keep flies out (US Army field sanitation).
Mark the spot so nobody digs there (US Army field sanitation).

list: Frozen ground and snow make cat holes hard to dig (Adirondack Mountain Club).
Snow is not a place to leave waste. Pack out solid waste and toilet paper (Leave No Trace, Adirondack Mountain Club).
If you can’t pack it out, bury it in a snow cat hole at least 200 feet (60 m) from trails and water (Leave No Trace). Check your map to see where the water is (Leave No Trace).

blocks.p: Wash your hands with soap and water, or use hand sanitizer when there is none (Leave No Trace).

sources.name: Leave No Trace, Winter Recreation
sources.used: Snow seems easy but isn’t the place for waste; pack out solid human waste; if unable, a snow cat hole 200 feet from trails and water

sources.name: US Forest Service, Going in the Forest
sources.used: Hole 4 to 6 inches wide and 6 to 8 inches deep; at least 200 feet (about 70 steps) from water, trails, parking areas and campsites; pack toilet paper out in a double zipper bag

sources.used: 6 to 8 inches deep, 4 to 6 inches across; 200 feet from water and trails (about 80 adult paces); disperse, don’t go to the same place twice; refill with the original dirt and disguise; pack out toilet paper; zipper bags or plastic containers sealed tight to pack out waste

sources.name: NYS DEC, State Land Camping Rules
sources.used: Use pit privies where provided; otherwise a hole 6 to 8 inches deep at least 150 feet from water or campsites, covered with leaves and soil; DEC notes Leave No Trace recommends 200 feet

sources.used: Frozen ground and snow make cat holes hard; pack out all solid human waste and toilet paper

sources.name: Public Health – Seattle & King County, How to create an emergency toilet
sources.used: Latrines not appropriate in urban locations; at least 100 feet from surface water and at least 100 feet downhill or away from any well, spring, home or campsite; away from food preparation and eating areas; hole at least 3 feet deep, bottom at least 1 foot above hard pan or water table; dirt, lime, mulch or ash after each use; cover between uses; keep covers closed; handwashing next to the toilet; supervise small children

sources.name: Sphere Handbook, 2018 edition (or later), Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene Promotion chapter (copy hosted by Universitas Sebelas Maret)
sources.used: At least 30 m from water sources and pit bottoms at least 1.5 m above the groundwater table without soil tests; not uphill or upwind of settlements; handwashing at toilets; 0.5 m at the top of the pit for backfill; increase the distances for fissured rock and limestone

sources.name: CDC, Potential Sanitation Solutions During an Emergency Response (December 2021)
sources.used: Trench latrines: narrow trenches with a temporary privacy structure, waste covered daily with soil, drainage to divert surface water, short life span, flooding in rain; pit latrines unsuitable where the water table is high; waste covered with soil when near full; handwashing stations at every sanitation facility

sources.name: Oregon State University Extension Service, Survival Basics: Sanitation and Waste Management (EM 9334, October 2021)
sources.used: Don’t bury waste within 100 feet of a water source; latrines for rural areas

sources.name: Jefferson County Department of Emergency Management with Clallam County Sheriff’s Emergency Management, Twin-Bucket Emergency Toilet (updated March 2015)
sources.used: Do not dig a pit privy in town: disease organisms contaminate neighboring properties

sources.used: Close a latrine pit when filled to within one foot of the top; fill to ground level packing the dirt; mound with soil to keep flies in or out; post a sign
